paragraphs.text: DevBridge – Developer Collaboration Platform
Krrish Kumar(23BCE0077)1, Anshu Khan(23BCE0115)2, Nupoor Mahajan(23BCE0040)3, Syamasudha Veeragandham4
1,2,3,4School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, Tamil Nadu, India – 632014
Email: 1krrish.kumar2023@vitstudent.ac.in, 2Anshu.khan2023@vitstudent.ac.in, 3nupooratul.mahajan2023@vitstudent.ac.in, 4syamasudha.v@vit.ac.in
Abstract

It's a common problem for student developers to find team members that are compatible for hackathons, startups, or collaborative software projects. Traditional networking platforms are centered around professional profiles and career advancement, providing dedicated functionality to help users build their professional network, limited recommendation features for skills, and no inbuilt support for team-building, workload recommendation, or project collaboration. Also, self-reported skills can make it challenging to determine whether a developer's skills are suitable for a project.

To address these problems, the DevBridge (Student Developer Collaboration Platform) is proposed in this paper, with the integration of developer discovery, multiple-objective teammate recommendation, and collaborative project management in a single application. The proposed method is based on the activity that developers have undertaken in GitHub, in addition to information related to their developer profiles, to create a more complete technical capability and interest representation, along with availability. The recommendation framework is inspired by the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), which takes into account multiple objectives such as developer expertise, project compatibility, and the workload balance to determine the best team of developers for each project. DevBridge also incorporates project task management, real-time communication, file sharing, contribution analytics and portfolio generation to support the entire collaborative project development lifecycle.

The proposed framework could be a full solution for the establishment of student teams and incorporation of evidence-based skill profiling, multi-objective optimization, collaboration tools. DevBridge seeks to provide a way to create more balanced teams, distribute workload more effectively, and have more transparency around the contribution of each person to the team's work. It also offers a structure to expand its recommendation functionality and to assess team formation strategies in various project scenarios.
Keywords: Student Developer Collaboration, Team Formation, Skill-Based Matching, Recommendation System, GitHub Integration, Real-Time Collaboration, Contribution Analytics, Hackathon Team Building
Introduction

Distributed software engineering and crowdsourced development paradigms have become vital models for software development in the planning, analysis, design, implementation and maintenance stages of a software lifecycle[1][2]. But, software development projects often suffer from schedule problems and difficulties in operation, with empirical evidence showing that more than 80% of software projects fall short of their expected delivery dates[3][4]. Thus, the proper selection of developers, team coordination, and sociotechnical alignment are essential prerequisites to maintain productivity and software quality in collaborative environments[3][6][7].

One of the ongoing challenges in a distributed engineering ecosystem or crowdsourced software platform is determining who should be responsible for a particular engineering task. Traditional task-posting and open call selection systems often fail to have good skill matches, have high task cancellation rates, and have high participant dropouts before tasks are completed (more than 14% on major competition platforms). The limitations of the recommendation frameworks that do not consider the skills of the developers in the development team, historical contribution patterns, and active task workloads of the team result in reduced output quality for project requesters and costly delivery delays[1].

This problem of finding effective collaborators is especially acute when a student developer community is looking for members to join them at a hackathon, in startup incubators, or to work on projects they are doing as free professionals. Current professional networking does not focus on the co-formation of skills in the moment between peers with similar technical interests, but rather on resume attribute and static career paths. Students are, therefore, missing out on having a dedicated platform to discover peers, and access to and use interactive engineering dev tools, where students have to wait on ad-hoc communication channels and unverified self-reported engineering skills[1].

Using CVs and self-proclaimed skill sets to determine potential collaborators just creates more skill redundancy and operational friction in development teams[8]. Empirical software engineering studies also show that studying actual coding activity, version control commits, and pull request histories from software repositories offer a much more accurate picture of the developer's actual technical skills and programming language ability[9]. Static resume data is not the same as dynamic developer profiling, which relies on activity. Dynamic developer profiling, based on activity data would, therefore, be essential in building balanced and effective software teams, rather than static data from resume[8].

Modern academic literature calls for the adoption of search-based models of multi-objective optimization, which consider the competencies of the developers, their expertise, the similarity of the tasks and distribution of workloads[1][8]. Also multi-objective evolutionary algorithms such

as NSGA – II have demonstrated that Pareto trade-off optimal solution sets that capture a compromise between conflicting performance criteria are superior to single performance perspective heuristics or even ‘static' classification models[1][10]. These principles of multi-objective recommender can be formally integrated into actual platforms for developers to create platforms that assemble skill-oriented teams using computers[1].

Considering this is a well-known problem in skill-based based matching and student-to-student skill-recommender system, a skill-based holistic solution is proposed called Student Developer Collaboration Platform (SDCP) or “DevBridge”. At DevBridge, they bypass the question of a resume and instead automatically generate dynamic profiles of your skills based on real coding repositories, commit histories and programming language usage with GitHub authentication. These are dynamic profiles that are subsequently compared to the technical interest self-identified by students and on the availability of other students, to provide a good foundation for the co-formation of student developers[1].

DevBridge introduces AI-based project and teammate recommendation that fares much better at matching student developers with projects/team-mates over a typical resume filter. This clever matchmaking mechanism studies the skill set, interests across the domain and availability of the developers and recommends optimum team-mix for participation in a hackathon, early stage of a startup project or freelance job offers. Nobody is hardcoded and only peers and candidates who fit the content in the student engineer's DevBridge profile are added to that student's list of discovered peers/candidates, thereby saving the engineering team admin time and accelerating the team formation process.

After discovering teammates good project execution needs a socio-technology supportive collaborative development environment[11][7]. DevBridge offers an integrated Kanban board along with task management, real – time chat with WebSockets and secure file sharing, keeping the workspace as uninterrupted as possible. Centralized system provides ongoing communication and structured tasks management during all software development lifecycle[8].

Through DevBridge's contribution analytics, the engagement and involvement of individual developers in teams are continually tracked, bringing transparency and clarity to the topic. Also, upon completion, it can generate developer portfolios for future collaborators, recruiters, and mentors to confirm that the developer has completed collaborative projects, and has verified his/her GitHub skills, even offering contribution analytics. The present invention is an automated portfolio generating system that converts collaborative work among peers to actual, peer reviewed, engineering achievements.

The main goals and limits for this project focus on the production of the core DevBridge platform, including integration with GitHub for authentication, dynamic profile extraction, AI matching features, real-time collaboration functionalities, tracking user contributions, and building of a portfolio using the implementation of production-ready tools: Spring Boot, Docker, WebSocket, MySQL and Hibernate. Advanced extensions like production payment integration for freelance

escrow and large-scale commercial deployments are clearly stated as future work and outside of the immediate project scope. DevBridge not only automatically matches players, but also has an integrated collaboration toolkit that allows to more easily assemble teams and gain insight into the progression of student developers in a scalable solution.
Research Objectives

Automate Dynamic Skill Profiling: Get commit history, coding activity, programming language used for different than static resumes, from a direct integration with a GitHub authentication, and construct a dynamic developer skill profile.
PH7C03: Implement Intelligent Peer Matchmaking: Employ an artificial intelligence (AI) system that matches student developers with skill sets and ensures peer match of technical interests and time.

Integrated Collaboration Workspace: Give a centralised socio-technical workspace with an interactive Kanban board, real-time WebSocket communication, file sharing and contribution analytics to optimise task management and monitor personal contributions.

Provide Verifiable Portfolio Generation: Develop an automated portfolio generator which converts complete collaborative projects and contribution metrics into verifiable credentials and deploy this in a production-ready technology stack (Spring Boot, Hibernate, MySQL, WebSocket, and Docker).
Related Work

The purpose of the foundational research paper for this project is to solve a critical problem in matching crowdsourced software development jobs with the right independent developers by transforming the problem into a multi – objective search – based optimization problem.The foundational research paper for this project is designed to solve a critical problem of matching the right developers with crowdsourced software development jobs by transforming the problem into a multi – objective search – based optimization problem. Traditional recommendation platforms often have high task cancellation rates, low candidate alignment, and only consider candidates based on a single perspective without taking into account developer capacity in real time. To address this, DRECT incorporates the Non – dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA – II) that aims at maximizing developer expertise and collaboration history, maximizing semantic similarity between developer skills and task requirements, and minimizing active developer workload to avoid developer burnout and project delivery delays [1]. DRECT outperforms traditional search techniques and state – of – the – art baselines by a factor of more than an order of magnitude, when evaluated on a real – world benchmark set of tasks from Topcoder that includes over 13,000 tasks and 8,000 developers, and shows that multi – objective optimization is a key paradigm for the modern distributed task allocation problem [1].

“RECAST (RECommendation Algorithm for Software Teams)” extends the concept of team level allocation, by automatically recommending full software development teams that meet certain role needs, technical skills and interpersonal compatibility [2]. RECAST tackles the challenge of project managers who have to choose project members from huge talent pools, by presenting team selection based on team – fitness scores computed from team collaboration history, task similarity, and skill sets represented as heterogeneous knowledge graphs. The framework uses a modified Max – Logit algorithm to intelligently prune the search space and to enumerate optimal team configurations without having to evaluate all possible combinations. Under exact – match evaluation protocols, RECAST has been tested on major open – source ecosystems (Apache, Atlassian and Moodle) and achieved a 646% increase in Mean Reciprocal Rank over the existing baselines.

The “WESTREC” dimensionally incorporates 5 effectiveness measures: historical collaboration, team cohesiveness, teammate interaction, member expertise, role experience [8] to recommend software teams automatically. Traditional recommendation algorithms are mainly aimed at individual roles, but not at assessing the overall team dynamics or the results of previous projects. WESTREC uses the project tracking systems (e.g. Jira) to build domain knowledge graphs, uses machine learning classification models to calculate the scores for possible team configurations, and employs a modified Max – Logit search algorithm to rank the possible team configurations. Empirical tests were conducted on large scale open source data sets, which verified that WESTREC is indeed significantly better than recency – based baselines at ranking previously successful winning teams for complex software tasks [8].

In the field of software crowdsourcing platforms, “TDMatcher” is designed to match the tasks of software enterprises with qualified software developers in the informal task description and the extreme cold start situation [6]. To deal with the unstructured task description, TDMatcher uses Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to obtain the latent feature topics and builds developer profiles from the past task contributions and social networks formed by developers. The platform treats task-developer matching as an optimization problem, and uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to stochastically evolve and diversify candidate matches. Experimental studies on real-world crowdsourcing data showed that TDMatcher not only outperforms frontier approaches in terms of prediction accuracy by 15%, but also in terms of recommendation diversity by 30%.

The “MUFFIN (Multi – Field Features representation and INteraction)” model is a candidate matching model for the larger recruitment markets that will solve the complex person – job fit problem by accurately predicting the match between a resume and a job description [12]. Traditional recruiters only consider textual similarity without taking into account key structured information like salary, location, or education. MUFFIN is able to overcome this limitation by separating numerical, categorical, and textual features into different fields, where textual features are embedded using a pre-trained ALBERT model and localized correlations are measured by a field inner interaction module. Moreover, a multi – head self – attention mechanism with residual
connections is used to capture global multi – field feature interactions, which allows the model to vastly outperform baseline recruitment deep learning models on real – world hiring datasets [12].

An AI system created by Alberola et al. is designed to optimize the composition of diverse student development teams in educational courses [13]. The tool is based on Belbin's role theory, which defines specific behavioural patterns that are required for team configurations to be balanced, thereby reducing interpersonal friction and increasing team productivity. The team allocation problem is mathematically formulated as a coalition structure generation problem and solved by using linear programming routines. The system dynamically updates the probabilities of students' roles as it goes, using peer – verified behavioral data rather than unreliable self – perception surveys, and incorporates peer feedback and iterative Bayesian learning after each project milestone [13].

In order to overcome the human resource constraint in complex software engineering pipeline, Chen et al. presented a multi – objective optimization model for multi – project IT development with dynamic competency evolution to assign multi – skilled technical staff to the development process [10]. The model incorporates an exponential learning and forgetting curve to continuously recalculate the individual productivity which is subject to change over time because of practice and disuse. The multi – project scheduling problem is defined as a problem that aims to satisfy three conflicting real – world managerial goals: maximize overall skill efficiency gain, minimize project cycle time, and minimize human resource expenditure. The framework is based on an adapted NSGA – II algorithm to produce Pareto – optimal schedules without any resource conflicts between hardware and software development activities, using serial schedule generation.

The modern world of code review seeks to suggest peer code reviewers for submitted changes on the basis of a history of code reviews rather than who wrote the source code [14]. cHRev understands that code ownership may not imply code review skills, and it uses three metrics to analyze past code review system log files: total number of review comments, number of active workdays spent reviewing a file, and recency of the contributions. Empirical testing on both open – source platforms and a commercial Microsoft codebase revealed that cHRev is significantly more effective than file – location tools that are used as a baseline (e.g., REVFINDER), which means that participation history in the review is a much better measure of reviewer expertise than the number of times they commit code [14].

To test the usefulness of such tools, Chouchen et al. performed a large – scale empirical study to assess the impact of automated code reviewer recommendation tools on developer decision – making in a commercial software setting [15]. The authors analyzed more than 21,000 code reviews conducted by JetBrains and surveyed qualitatively across JetBrains and Microsoft on developer adoption, and compared the relationship between the offline accuracy measures and developer adoption. The study found that the general impression of the accuracy of automated recommendations is positive, but developers are not often able to use these in their normal workflow because they typically know their desired reviewer before creating the task. These

findings underscore the need for context – aware and user – centric recommendation systems that can overcome the real collaboration constraints in place instead of supplanting known peer relationships[15].

de Lima Júnior et al. [9] wanted to find a way to automate the process of assigning core integrators to incoming pull requests in pull – based software development workflows, to address the problem of code review bottlenecks in open source projects. The authors took 32 free software projects on GitHub to study; they gathered a wide body of attributes from the history of the requester, social connections, file paths and the activity of the developer's for the requesting project. Supervised feature selection and training – test sliding window validation were used in the study to determine which features offer the highest predictive power for integrator selection: these include features like RequesterLogin, FilePaths and ActiveDeveloper. The optimized classification model achieved as high as 54% improvement in the normalized precision with the ability to effectively reduce the important repository management [9].

Mao et al. gave a comprehensive literature review to identify a sound taxonomy and mapping of Crowdsourced Software Engineering (CSE) throughout the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) [5]. The survey by systematically reviewing more than 200 publications defined CSE as the process of software engineering work that is performed externally via open calls to online worker pools. The authors classified the current research in the fields of requirement engineering, design, coding, testing, and maintenance, and uncovered the key trends in the industry and some recurring operational issues. The survey highlighted that although crowdsourcing is faster and cheaper, the key elements of the platform's success are automated task allocation, quality control systems and maintaining the motivation of the crowd workers [5].

Vasilescu et al. performed an empirical study to classify the use of external crowd knowledge by software engineers in Stack Overflow discussions in the context of GitHub code commits [16]. The authors categorized the usage of the developer crowd in 14 different technical topics by crawling the active repositories from GitHub that include explicit references to posts from Stack Overflow in their commit logs. The results showed that the main reason for using crowd platforms is to gain programming language skills, to understand how to use the APIs, to solve web framework problems, and to document software bugs. The study showed that crowdsourced Q&A communities are an integral part of the technical documentation, and they have a direct impact on the daily version control processes[16].

Al-Subaihin et al. [17] carried out an empirical study to assess the potential of using natural language processing and feature extraction techniques to automatically cluster mobile applications using textual store descriptions. Analyzing over 12,000 Android apps from Google Play, the authors evaluated five text similarity detection techniques – including Vector Space Models (VSM), Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and dependency – based sentence parsing. The study demonstrated that traditional app store classification is inadequate in terms of capturing functional software similarities using hierarchical agglomerative classification validated against human

ground truth. The results showed that the advanced dependency – based feature extraction and topic modeling were significantly outperforming the baseline methods and giving an effective blueprint for mining textual software descriptions[17].

Gharehyazie et al. studied social dynamics in open-source governance in order to understand what factors best predict the transition to trusted core developer (committer) status for developers in projects hosted by the Apache Software Foundation [7]. The authors gathered two-way communication metrics from developer mailing lists and version control commit histories for six major Apache projects, and analyzed the data. The statistical models showed that the number of two-way messages and messages initiated by discussion is a significantly better predictor of committership than the number of code patches submitted. In addition, there is a clear social ramping up before the initiation and social ramping down after the initiation when write access is granted [7].

In the context of technical co-development, Gharehyazie and Filkov attempted to follow implicit, self – organized group cooperation in large open – source projects by examining the multi – developer commit synchronization [3]. The authors investigated 26 Apache projects, and created an algorithmic approach to identifying instances of group co-development, in which three or more programmers modified the same software packages at similar times. The study validated that distributed teamwork happens naturally in large codebases, but not as often as one might expect by chance because of the overhead of coordination. Interestingly, the developers in the collaborative groups showed altered coding conduct, and increased code submission rates per time unit than those of the developers who worked alone [3].

Lindsjørn et al. conducted an empirical survey to quantify the effect of Teamwork Quality (TWQ) on the performance of agile software teams, the individual learning, and the work satisfaction of team members [11] by focusing on the execution metrics at team level. The authors surveyed 477 people across 71 agile development teams on six key constructs of TWQ: communication, coordination, balance of member contributions, mutual support, effort, and cohesion. The results of the structural equation modeling showed that teamwork quality, team member learning, and work satisfaction had a strong positive relationship. The study revealed, however, that there was a significant perceptual gap; TWQ was highly correlated with the performance ratings of internal team members and team leaders, but was not correlated with the performance ratings from external product owners [11].

In order to reduce the risk of software problems with scheduled due dates, Choetkiertikul et al. proposed a predictive model that attempts to determine if software problems with planned due dates will miss their deadlines [4]. The authors mined historical issue tracking data from eight large open – source projects, such as JIRA, and identified 19 different risk factors, including developer workload, discussion length, priority changes, and version re – assignment. The predictive models, using L1 – penalized logistic regression for feature selection, had a precision of 79% and an AUC of 83% in predicting the likelihood and severity of delay. The study confirmed
that the most common risk indicators for all codebases were developer workload and discussion time, which means that issue repository mining can identify project bottlenecks in advance [4].

On the subject of collective decision-making, Chen et al. designed a group recommendation method which predicts group preferences by simulating interpersonal interaction among group members [18]. However, a standard recommendation system is not appropriate for group settings since it is unable to handle collective input or understand the effect that group members have on collective purchasing decisions. The proposed method is a hybrid of item – based collaborative filtering and genetic algorithm (GA) to solve the data sparsity problem without the need for expert surveys. The genetic algorithm is used to learn the member influence weights and member interaction dynamics from a set of known ratings for subgroups, which allows the system to accurately predict a group's collective rating for new items, while capturing the personalities of the members [18].

Group preference aggregation is also addressed in [19] in which Wang et al. proposed a member contribution – based group recommendation (MC-GR) approach for maximizing satisfaction in random groups based on rating data only. To overcome this problem, the system proposes a Member Contribution Score (MCS) model based on separable non – negative matrix factorization (SNMF) to assess the representative status of each user in a group profile, without requiring additional social metadata. Further, a local average rating (LA) model based on Manhattan distance further improves predictions by reducing fat – tail rating distortions. Experimental results showed that the MC – GR model is able to balance conflicting member preferences and it performs significantly better than the traditional aggregation models (such as least – misery or average rating) [19].

Lastly, for the field of distributed multi-agent decision systems, Dai et al. explored game – theoretic learning algorithms for the solution of a joint base station selection and resource allocation problem in a complex wireless communication network [20]. The authors modeled the resource allocation problem as a potential game, both exactly and as a state – based potential game, to tackle the NP-hardness of maximizing system throughput when the computation is complex. The distributed agents are able to reach stochastically stable Nash equilibria that correspond to near – optimal system throughput by using heterogeneous exploration rates in the Max – logit learning algorithms. This framework demonstrates the efficient exploration of complex, high – dimensional multi – objective decision spaces by search – based stochastic learning algorithms, without the need for centralized communication overhead [20].

While there have been marked improvements in team recommendation algorithms and crowdsourced task allocation systems, there are three important gaps in the existing literature and software tools that are evident: (1) current tools and literature rely on static resumes or unverified self-reported qualifications, which do not reflect a candidate's dynamic technical growth; (2) there is a significant degree of tool fragmentation, between the discovery, communication, and project tracking tools; and (3) no automated mechanisms for peer – verified credentialing exist. As a result,

the student software developer may encounter significant challenges when trying to assemble well-rounded, dependable teams to participate in hackathons, startup incubators and freelance projects; often they are unable to determine if the participants have the appropriate skills to complete the projects or maintain a structured project development process, and may experience skill mismatch, dropouts and project schedule overruns. “DevBridge” provides an integrated collaboration ecosystem that validates directly against GitHub and builds dynamic, activity – based skill profiles based on real version control history, commit patterns and programming language usage, to address these literature gaps and solve the fundamental challenge of student developer co-formation. DevBridge features an AI – powered matchmaking system that matches compatible peers by verified skills, domain interests, and active workloads, and offers a single workspace with real – time WebSocket communication, Kanban task management, and contribution analytics that automatically turn completed collaborative work into verifiable, peer – reviewed developer portfolios.

Materials and Methods
Research Methodology

The proposed DevBridge platform is based on the design and implementation approach to solve the problems of student developer discovery, team formation and collaborative software development. The methodology combines developer profile construction, project requirement analysis, multi-objective teammate recommendation and a common collaboration workspace.

DRECT is used to inform the system design, which is based on a multi-objective search problem formulation and the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) that balances developer expertise, task similarity, and workload.

DevBridge is not just a developer recommendation system that uses static resumes or technical attributes alone, but one that integrates technical skills, programming interests, project needs, availability, and collaboration information. Developer profiles can be enriched with metadata from the developer's GitHub repository and statistics for the developer's programming languages, depending on the API permissions set and the availability of such data. Project owners define the skills, interests, roles and number of people expected in a project team. The recommendation component assesses the eligible developers and helps to select the candidate teams which will provide a balance of technical compatibility and workload.
The methodology consists of six major stages:
Developer registration and profile acquisition
Project requirement specification
Data preprocessing and feature extraction
Multi-objective team recommendation
Collaborative project execution
Evaluation of the recommendation process and application functionality.
The results of the recommendation stage are a list of the candidates, or teams of candidates, ranked by their suitability, with explanations of why they are suitable.

The methodology is modular to allow the evaluation of the recommendation component without the need to evaluate the other platform services. This separation allows the algorithm that recommends the best items to be contrasted with simpler baselines, without claiming the improvements to be linked to other features like messaging or task management.
Data Acquisition
Data Sources
DevBridge needs consistent information on developers, projects, skills and workloads.
There are four main data types in the proposed data model.

Developer profile information: Developers can include a unique identifier, technical skills, preferred domains of development, experience level, availability, and history of project participation in their developer profile. If a user has GitHub integration, their repository metadata, programming language statistics and contribution activity can be included in their profile.

Project requirement information: Project record can include project identifier, textual description, required programming languages, technical skills, project domain, required team size, preferred developer roles and project status. These characteristics set the criteria by which candidate developers are judged.

Collaboration data: Historical data will be used to estimate familiarity with collaboration if it exists, if it does not, it will not be used. If there is no historical data from which to measure, then the compatibility of collaboration should be assumed to be not available, or measured by a clearly defined proxy, not by a historical relationship.

Workload and availability data: Data about workload can include the number of projects and/or tasks that are active for a developer. Availability can be indicated by declared weekly hours, categorical availability or other field supported by the application. These features will help the recommendation process not pick technically appropriate developers who can't be reasonably involved.

The main source of data should be the data stored in the DevBridge application and any external source that the system implemented can successfully access. The DRECT paper relies on historical Topcoder tasks and developer records, which should not be considered as the DevBridge dataset without explicitly obtaining and using the data in the experiments.

Data Preprocessing
Data acquired should be checked for correctness before score recommendations are made. The preprocessing procedure includes the following operations:
Data validation: Check required project attributes and mandatory identifiers. Avoid accepting or marking as a developer record or project when a developer record or project can't be found.
Duplicate removal: Find duplicate records, based on stable identifiers and appropriate uniqueness constraints.
Handling missing values: Identify missing values from true zeros. Not having workload and/or collaborative data does not imply low workload or compatibility.
Skill normalization: Normalize skill names and labels for programming languages using a controlled mapping e.g. aliases common to a language, capitalisation.
Feature encoding: Represent categorical features in uniform representations, and map numeric features to comparable ranges.
When calculating semantic similarity, the project description, skill description is text pre-processed (normalized), irrelevant formatting is removed, and a feature vector is created from the text.
Historical consistency: Only information in the system when the recommendation is being considered.

Documentations need to be provided in case data is acquired from GitHub and APIs fail, repositories cannot be accessed, rate limits are enforced, and profiles are missing. If your external request is not successful don't write it off as a lack of skill on the developer's part.
1.3 System Architecture

DevBridge is a modular and multi-layer application, that links developer profile management with project management, recommendation services and collaborative tools. There are five logical layers in the architecture.

The top level would be the presentation layer of the site, from the owner interface, registration and login information, developer accounts, project creation, finding other teammates, task management, communication and the developer's portfolio.

Application and authentication layer: Processes user requests, validates data, manages sessions/tokens, applies authorisation and controls interactions between the user interface and the backend services.

Profile and project management layer: maintains and stores the developer's profile, project requirements, skills, prior participation history, status and availability of tasks. When combined, GitHub Integration provides an extra piece of profile proof.

Recommendation and analytics layer: Performs the pre-processing of the profile and project attributes, calculates the developer to project match and analyzes the developer project team candidates and outputs the ranked developer project recommendations. Contribution analytics may be based on one or multiple events, such as tasks, repository, or other metrics.

Persistence and integration layer: Stores the application records into the application database defined and manages the connection with external services. Where implemented, real time communication, file storage and deployment services are integrated into it.

Recommendation service needs to be decoupled from profile and project management to allow different recommendation algorithms to be compared against the same set of input records. This modular design also facilitates independent testing and replacement of the individual components.
Recommendation Problem Formulation

Suppose that (D = {d1, d2, …, dN}) is the set of developers who are eligible to submit a project for recommendation, and (p) is the project that is submitted for recommendation. The project defines a set of skills that are required (Sp), a desired team size (k), and any applicable eligibility constraints.

The aim is to select a candidate team (T ⊆ D) that is technically appropriate, is perfectly team compatible and has a even distribution of labour. Three objectives are taken into account in the proposed adaptation:
Maximize developer expertise and collaboration compatibility.
Maximize developer–project similarity.
Minimize the workload of the selected developers.
These goals are based on the conceptual framework of DRECT[1] but their operational definitions need to be tailored to the attributes in DevBridge.
Skill Compatibility
Let Sp be the set of skills that are required for a project and Sd be the set of skills that are associated with a developer (d). The Jaccard similarity is used to define a basic skill-overlap score:
SkillSim(d, p) = |Sd ∩ Sp| / |Sd ∪ Sp|

If the union is not empty, the score is in the range [0, 1]. A score of one means that the skills are the same, and a score of zero means that there are no skills in common. If both sets are empty, the score is considered undefined and the record is marked for the score, but not automatically awarded a perfect match.
Where evidence strength or skill importance is available, a weighted alternative can be used: WSS(d, p) = sum{s ∈ Sp} (ws · e{d,s}) / sum{s ∈ Sp} ws

In this case, (ws) is the importance of the required skill (s), and (e{d,s} ∈ [0,1]) is the evidence-based proficiency score for developer (d). The weighted score is only defined if the denominator is positive and the evidence values are consistently normalized. A GitHub language percentage does not measure individual proficiency in a language, but rather evidence of the use of a language in a repository.
Developer–Project Similarity

Text vectors can be used to represent project descriptions and developer skill or interest descriptions. When TF–IDF is used to extract features, the cosine similarity between a developer representation (vd) and a project representation (vp) is:
TextSim(d, p) = (vd · vp) / (|vd|2 · |vp|2)
This score reflects the text similarity between the two representations. When either of the vectors is zero, it is undefined and should be treated separately.
A joint compatibility score can be defined as:
C(d, p) = α · SkillSim(d, p) + β · TextSim(d, p) + γ · InterestSim(d, p)

where (α, β, γ ≥ 0) and (α + β + γ =1). If interest data and the scoring method are not available, then the interest similarity term cannot be included. The weights should not be adjusted to yield a desired test result, but should be given beforehand or determined through training or validation data.
Expertise and Collaboration Objective

Let (E(d,p) ∈ [0,1]) be the normalized evidence of developer expertise for project (p) for a candidate team (T). Suppose that (H(di,dj) ∈ [0,1]) is the observed collaboration compatibility between two developers (di) and (dj), if available.
A potential team goal is:
In this case, the relative influence of collaboration is controlled by (λ). The pairwise term is only defined for teams of size 2 or more, and is skipped or treated separately for teams of size 1.

If there is no history of collaboration observed for a new platform, (H) should not be shown as a historical score. This term may be omitted or may be provided by a clearly defined alternative compatibility feature, or it may be reported as unavailable if collaboration data is not available.
Team–Project Similarity Objective
For a team (T) with (k=|T|) members, the average developer–project similarity is:
f2(T) = (1 / k) · sum{d ∈ T} C(d, p)
A separate measure of skill coverage can be included to reward complementary expertise: Coverage(T, p) = sum{s ∈ Sp} (ws · I[∃ d ∈ T, s ∈ Sd]) / sum{s ∈ Sp} ws

where (𝐼[⋅]) is 1 if the condition is true and 0 if it is not. The coverage is a measure of the representation of required skills throughout the team, while the average similarity is a measure of individual alignment. If the algorithm implemented requires the use of the coverage term, then that term should be introduced as a separate objective or explicitly included in (f2).
Workload Minimization Objective
Let a(d) be the number of active projects or tasks of developer (d). The normalized workload value can be computed as:
W(d) = min(1, a(d) / Amax)
where Amax > 0 is a pre-defined workload normalization threshold. This formulation can be used for a bounded workload feature but it is not a measure of a developer's actual available hours.
The objective for the team is:
f3(T) = (1 / k) · sum{d ∈ T} W(d)

The algorithm for recommendation minimizes (f3). If there is an additional availability constraint or score, it may be added if declared availability is available. The number of projects should not be confused with the number of projects declared available as it does not necessarily indicate the effort.
Multi-objective Optimization
The team recommendation problem is expressed as:
Maximize: f1(T), f2(T) Minimize: f3(T)
Subject to: T ⊆ D, |T| = k, eligibility and availability constraints

The goals may be in opposition. For instance, the developer who has the best technical score may be already working on a few projects, whereas a less experienced developer might be more available. Such trade-offs can be masked by a single weighted score. NSGA-II, on the other hand, looks for non-dominated candidate teams, so that multiple trade-offs can be kept.

A candidate team (Ta) dominates team (Tb) if (Ta) achieves at least as good an outcome on each of the objectives and a better outcome on at least one of the objectives, in the maximization or minimization direction respectively. The non-dominated solutions are arranged in a Pareto front and the final recommendation list can be obtained from this front.
NSGA-II-Based Recommendation Algorithm

In the reference study DRECT, multiple objective functions are used to search for candidate developer sets using NSGA-II [1]. DevBridge can take this route for team recommendation if the implementation does include the respective evolutionary operators and objective evaluation.

Each chromosome represents a team of (k) different eligible developers in the team-selection representation. The three objectives of Section 3.4 are used to evaluate a chromosome. The algorithm creates a set of candidate teams, applies non-dominated sorting to rank the solutions, and applies crowding distance to maintain diversity of solutions on the same Pareto front.The proposed algorithm is as follows.
Algorithm 1: Multi-objective developer team recommendation
Input: Eligible developer set (D), project requirements (p), required team size (k), population size (P), maximum generation count (G), crossover probability (pc), and mutation probability (pm).
Output: A ranked list of candidate developer teams.
Verify project requirements and eliminate developers who are not qualified.
Identify and standardize existing developer and project features.
Check that there are still (k) eligible developers.
Create a population (Q0) of (P) valid candidate teams.
Evaluate (f1), (f2), and (f3) for every candidate team.
For each generation (g = 1, …, G):
Sort the current population in a non-dominated way.
Compute crowding distance in each Pareto front.
Use rank and diversity information to select parents.
Apply crossover with probability (pc).
Randomly apply mutation with probability (pm).
Fix any invalid chromosome to make sure that there are unique and eligible team members and the team size.
Assess the product of the breeding population.
Combine parent and offspring populations.
Select the next generation using non-dominated rank and crowding distance.
Remove the non-dominated candidate teams from the final population.
Eliminate duplicate recommendations, and use eligibility checks.
Document and rank or present the resulting candidate teams.
Provide the recommendations along with their objective scores and explanations that are available. Bring the recommendations back including objective scores and explanations for each recommendation.

The following situations are acceptable cases for the algorithm: lack of competent developers, lack of some features, repetition of some members of the team and some of the requirements of the project are wrong. Where it is not feasible to form a valid team, the service should return an appropriate response, not a 'faux pas' recommendation.
The values (P), (G), (pc), and (pm) should be recorded in the experimental set-up. Should not be reported until after implementation has been inspected and experiments have been performed.

Experimental Design
Application Functional Testing

Functional testing is used to determine if each feature implemented is working as it should. The test suite should include tests for registration and login, profile updates, project creation, recommendation requests, team selection, task operations, and collaboration features (if
applicable). Initial conditions, expected outcome, observed outcome and pass/fail should be recorded for each test.
Recommendation Evaluation

If reliable labels are available, the quality of the recommendations can be compared to the developer–project assignments in the past. The recommended developers are compared with the relevant developers in the held-out reference records for each project. The metrics that can be used are Precision@k, Recall@k, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and hypervolume and convergence-related metrics for multi-objective optimization.

When there are timestamps in the historical records, it is better to have a temporal split, where the earlier records are used to build profiles and train or configure the method, and the later records are used for evaluation. This decreases the chance of predicting past assignments with future contributions.

For a project with a sufficiently large set of independent, labelled examples, a training/validation/test split of 70%/15%/15% might be considered. This ratio is a suggested split, not an actual split. Splitting should be done at an appropriate project or temporal level, to minimize leakage from repeated developers, duplicate projects or overlapping historical activity. If the data set is small, a chronological holdout could be more defensible, as could a grouped cross validation.

Without a defensible relevance label, Precision@k, Recall@k, and MRR cannot be used as empirical measures of accuracy. If user evaluations are carried out, they are carefully designed and reported, as will be functional tests, objective score behaviour, runtime and feasibility, if applicable. Synthetic examples test the implementation but not the effectiveness of suggestions in reality.
Baseline Comparison
Eligible candidates and project requirements should be the same for both the simple baselines and proposal about the approach to the recommendations. Suitable baselines include:
Random recommendation: Randomly chooses developers that are eligible, with team size limitations.
Skill-overlap ranking: Ranks candidates according to similarity of their skills to project requirements.
Weighted-score recommendation: Ranks candidates based on a set of defined skill, interest and workload features.
NSGA-II recommendation: If implemented, searches for candidate teams balancing the defined objectives.

All methods should use the same evaluation records and relevance definitions. If stochastic algorithms are being evaluated, results should be averaged over a number of runs and variability reported if possible. Comparisons should not suggest that one algorithm is better than another without the evidence of experiments.
Evaluation Metrics
Precision@k
Precision@k measures the proportion of the top-(k) recommendations that are relevant:
Precision@k = |Rk ∩ G| / |Rk|

The set of the top-(k) recommended developers and the set of relevant developers in the evaluation ground truth (G). The higher the number, the less irrelevant recommendations will be in the list shown.
Recall@k
Recall@k measures the proportion of relevant developers retrieved among the top-(k) recommendations:
Recall@k = |Rk ∩ G| / |G|

The higher the value, the more of the known relevant developers are included in the recommendation list. Precision and recall must be read together, as a method can be better at improving one at the cost of the other.
Mean Reciprocal Rank
MRR measures how early the first relevant developer appears in a ranked list:

Here, (Q) is the number of evaluated recommendation queries, and (rq) is the rank of the first relevant result for query (q). The reciprocal rank of a query is zero if there is no relevant result in the list of results evaluated. The higher the MRR, the sooner the relevant results will be found.
Hypervolume
Hypervolume measures the volume of the objective space covered by the Pareto front obtained compared to a given reference point. It is a useful tool for assessing multi-objective

optimizers as it captures convergence and diversity. Objective directions and normalization need to be consistent and the reference point need to be recorded. Hypervolume values are only meaningful when compared with other values under comparable objective definitions and normalization procedures.
Runtime
Runtime is the time elapsed to produce recommendations in a given environment and configuration:
Tavg = (1 / M) · sum{i=1}^{M} Ti

where (M) is the number of runs repeated and (Ti) is the time for run (i). When comparing methods, the number of candidates, population size, number of generations, hardware and implementation environment should be kept constant or reported.
Functional Test Pass Rate
The functional test pass rate is the number of test cases that pass the test divided by the total number of test cases that were run:
PassRate = (Npassed / Nexecuted) · 100
This metric is used to assess correctness of implementation for the scenarios being tested, but not the quality of teammates' recommendations.
Fault Handling and Reproducibility

The application should check user input and explicitly deal with operational failures. Examples are a user who doesn't have the skill or resources, too small or too big a team, there aren't any fit users who can develop it, the user's GitHub profile can't be found, user's API rate limit is reached, user submits the same project twice or more, or the user gets no recommendation.

The system needs to provide a helpful error message for every error, to log an appropriate diagnostic event (without revealing credentials or sensitive information), and to not return wrong suggestions. A bounded retry policy might be used for transient failures of external services; validation errors should not be retried by the external service, but should be returned to the user.

The experimental report should contain information on the source and date of data, rules used for data preprocessing, rules used for the features definition, objective weights, random seed, algorithm parameters, evaluation protocol, and software and hardware versions and the number of
repeated runs for reproducing results. Personal data stored in datasets should be accessed in appropriate ways and protected in a way that ensures privacy.

To sum up, the proposed methodology is associated with student developer profiling, project requirement analysis, multi-objective team recommendation and collaborative project execution. Experimentally valid requires appropriate data, accurate execution of the recommendation algorithm, leakage-aware evaluation, and clear reporting of results observed. The final methodology should be correlated with the implemented DevBridge source code prior to its presentation as a completed experimental system.

Discussion

The DevBridge methodology proposed in this article overcomes the shortcomings of informal communication or limited technical skills matching to select project teammates. The system takes into account the needs of the project, the skills of the developers and the amount of work.

The use of NSGA-II offers a guide to exploring multiple objectives and to determining non-dominated candidate teams. This is particularly true if the technically best (or worst) developers are not the most available ones. The quality of the recommendations, however, is contingent upon the completeness and reliability of the developer profiles, and the appropriateness of the objective functions.

The site also recommends a general area to find developers to collaborate on projects with together. A fusion of recommendation, project management and contribution tracking may decrease the amount of tools required to handle these activities. But, in practice, such an integration will need to be shown to have value by the user in practicing it and in the evaluation.

There is a lack of empirical measurements in the present work, one of the disadvantages. The following statistics have not been demonstrated in an experiment: Dataset statistics, Recommendation accuracy, Execution time, Scalability, User satisfaction. The implementation and testing should be performed on a repeatable and documented data set and evaluation criteria and compared to the baseline method – future.

Last but not least, this section explains the planned assessment framework and activities of DevBridge. It specifies what is needed to test the proposed system functionally, compares it with the existing system, and defines mechanisms to handle faults. The platform's effectiveness and the capability of the recommendation algorithm have yet to be empirically validated.
Limitations and Future Work
Limitations

The proposed DevBridge platform is a conceptual structure for students to collaborate with each other as developers and for teammates to be recommended. But there are a few restrictions to keep in mind.
No prototype: Proposed system has not been implemented or tested in practice. So it is not verified to be correct in function, to be recommended and usable in practice.

Profiles of developers: The value of teammates' recommendations is dependent on the accuracy and completeness of developer profiles, which include technical skills, interests, availability and past project experience. Information that is incomplete or out-of-date can lead to inappropriate recommendations.

Limited empirical evaluation: There is no experimental data, measured performance value, or result of user evaluation. Therefore, the quantitative assessment of the effectiveness of the proposed recommendation methodology is not possible yet.

Computational complexity: The proposed NSGA-II-based multi-objective optimization approach may need more computational resources with the increase in the number of developers, project requirements, and optimization objectives. It's not scalable and has not been tested for execution times.

Focusing on collaboration factors less: Technical expertise, project compatibility, and workload are important factors in team formation but may not necessarily reflect interpersonal compatibility, communication skills, learning objectives, or individual working preferences.

External service and security dependencies: If integrating external services like GitHub, there are API availability, access permissions and data consistency risks. Implementation and testing of authentication, authorization and privacy protection, secure handling of data would also need to be implemented and tested.
Future Work
The proposed DevBridge methodology will be developed in the future into a practical and experimentally verified platform.

User authentication, developer profile management, project creation and recommending team members are the decisive elements of the platform that are also realized in the prototype. An adequate application and/or database architecture can be achieved to provide required functions.

Incorporation and validation of the dataset: The development or acquisition of a structured dataset should proceed in an appropriate manner with the necessary consent and privacy protection, including developer's competences, project expectations and requirements, availability of the developer, and experiences in collaborations. Recommendations may be validated and preprocessed to be more reliable.

The NSGA-II approach should be implemented and the evaluation of the recommendation algorithm should be done with random selection, skill-based ranking and weighted-score methods. Precision, recall, skill-match quality, workload balance, execution time, and diversity of recommended teams (where appropriate ground-truth data are available) can be taken into account for evaluation.

Scalability and optimization: Future experiments should try the algorithm with different number of developers and demands of the project. Other parameter tuning and optimization can be done to help cut computational cost without losing the efficacy of the recommendations.

Some other features include integrating with GitHub, tracking of contributions, monitoring of project progress, communication , and developer feedback. All of these characteristics can be used in the collaboration process following forming team.

Relevance, usability, fairness and overall satisfaction of the recommendations could be evaluated in a student developer pilot with User-centred evaluation The feedback from the participants might be incorporated into the criteria and interface of the recommendations.

Privacy/safety/fairness: Security in accessing, authentication, reduction of data and clarity of criteria for recommendations. The system should also be tested and be made sure that it doesn't discriminate the developers if he doesn't have complete profile or previous experience in it.
Conclusion

DevBridge suggests an all-encompassing Student Developer Collaboration Platform to solve problems faced by finding appropriate teammates, balancing development teams and coordinating collaborative software projects. Students, developers want something more specific than job postings and user profiles on a professional networking site that considers technical skills, project requirements, interests, and availability. DevBridge aims to close these loopholes by creating one holistic platform, that incorporates features such as developer discovery, intelligent teammate recommendations and collaboration with projects.

The proposed approach combines developer profiling based on developer's repository in GitHub with the traditional approach to support the developers' portfolio with information regarding the technical skills through additional evidence in the developer's repository, programming language used and activity in the repository. The platform is designed to match the right candidates with the needs of specific projects and developers, based on these qualities. Moreover, integration of the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (II) NSGA-II allows to consider multiple objectives, such as developer knowledge, project compatibility and workload balance. This multi-objective method is aimed at allowing a greater flexibility on the teams to be created, considering the compromise between being technically appropriate and heavily loaded with developers.

However, DevBridge also has an inbuilt collaboration platform that includes project task management, instant messaging, file sharing, developer portfolio, contribution analytics, and a lot more that can be suggested by teammates. These capabilities can help to minimize reliance on standalone tools and streamline the collaborative software development process. Additional elements feature contribution analytics and portfolio generation that may be useful for the student to demonstrate their contributions to projects and therefore the development experience they have had beyond projects to would-be collaborators, mentors and recruiters.

Overall, DevBridge introduces a structured solution to better student developer collaboration, through evidence-based skill profiling, multi-objective optimization, and project management features. Its modular design offers a structure to expand the recommendation system and add more co-operation functionality as needs change. Future works include the actual implementation of the proposed modules, comparison of the proposed recommendation algorithm to the baseline approach, performance and scalability analysis, and user feedback for usability and relevance of the recommendations. More work in the area of fairness of recommendations, data privacy, and the trustworthiness of skills that can be derived from GitHub would benefit the platform.

Finally, DevBridge is a potential framework to help students form teams based on skills and work together on software development. The platform's features are designed to streamline student collaboration, improve the organization and visibility of different activities, and ensure that the project's objectives are met. It is important that it has to be put into practice and be systematically assessed in various academic and development settings to determine its effectiveness.
